testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Otoe Sub-agency, Red Rock, Oklahoma
testimony.subject: Condition of Indians before and after receiving patents-in-fee
testimony.key_claims: Fee patent Indians are in worse condition than when under Government jurisdiction. Indians who received patents sold land, bought expensive automobiles, spent money on gambling. Old dependent Indians receiving $100 monthly can scarcely exist. Indians are dissatisfied and believe government employees are in league with grafters. Recommends turning loose able-bodied and educated Indians but establishing community system for uneducated and old dependent ones with 20 acres reserved for home. Successful examples include Harold Barnes, Jacob Blackhawk, James Arkeketa, Henry Black, George W. Dailey, Blaine Faw Faw, David Pettit, Berth Tillman, Sam Lincoln.

testimony.subject: Fee patent Indians at Pawnee
testimony.key_claims: Indians questioned about release from federal control stated they are not satisfied, in bad financial shape, and feel government should not have released them. Indians mortgaged or sold land immediately upon receiving patent-in-fee, purchased expensive autos and lived high. Suggests older Indians be kept under government control while younger Indians should be given competency rights. Believes sooner younger Indians are released, sooner Indian problem will be solved. Suggests reserving 40 acres of original allotment as home site.

testimony.witness_title: Agent Farmer, Pawnee Agency, Pawnee, Oklahoma
testimony.subject: Fee patent Indians at Pawnee
testimony.key_claims: Indians who received fee patents sold land and spent all money, are in debt. Very few who received patents still own their allotments - not one out of ten have not sold. Recommends issuing fee patent for part of allotment and holding at least 40 acres in trust. Names of those doing well: Louis Matlock, Elmo Jim, Eva N. Cummings. Names of those who have not gained: Clarance Field, Wallace Murie, Caroline Murie, Maggie Knife Chief, Thomas Hand, John Howell, Maude Hand. Those doing well who still hold land: Emmit Pearson, George Gover, Frank Rouwalk.

testimony.subject: Patented Indians - Sac & Fox and Iowa Indians
testimony.key_claims: Patented Indians have disposed of allotments and are compelled to labor. Not as easy for Indian to secure position as white man. One Indian worked for one company for three or four years. About 81 patents given out four or five years ago, not more than 10 still have their land. Some heired lands remain. Children do not have necessaries of life. Does not think advisable to turn all Indians loose at once. Suggests allowing Indians to dispose of heired lands but hold own allotments.

testimony.subject: Cheyenne and Arapahoe Indians and fee patents
testimony.key_claims: Has worked three years with Cheyenne and Arapahoe Indians. Knows of only a few who kept land after receiving patent. Nearly all sell as soon as they can make sale, spend money, are satisfied, go to work and make better citizens. Does not think it good policy to turn all Indians loose from Government control at once. Suggests young boys and girls who finish education should have property turned over. Indians should be expected to take care of themselves. Lists Indians farming successfully under government control: David Bighead, Harry Bates, Walter Fire, Dan Tucker.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Spokane Indian Agency, Wellpinit, Washington
testimony.subject: Fee patents and releasing Indians from Government supervision on Spokane Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Pretty well in accord with Office policy but does not think good to make all Indians of half or less Indian blood citizens at once. Each case should be decided on merits considering educational qualifications, business experience, degree of Indian blood, robustness, and age. Spokane allotments mostly 80 acres, not good quality, mostly timber. Many allotments worth only $400-$800. Recommends 20-40 acres held in trust for home site. 112 Indians received fee patents; 54 retained allotments, 48 sold them. Most sold soon after receiving patents. Indians who retained land are generally doing as well as before.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Spokane Indian Agency, Wellpinit, Washington
testimony.subject: Condition of patent-in-fee Indians on Spokane Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Larger percent of fee patent Indians doing as well as before. Quite a few sold land but larger percent used money to good advantage. Percentage who spent money without good returns no larger than any other race. Most are satisfied with patents. Would use same policy Department has been using, examine each individual case. Would release all allotments on this reservation because each is small. Provides names and addresses of those who sold and those who retained land.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, United States Indian Service, Poteau, Oklahoma
testimony.subject: Full removal of restrictions on Choctaw Indians in Five Tribes
testimony.key_claims: Government work in Five Tribes has been to divide common estate and vest individually. Future business will be with individuals. Should focus on fitting individual Indian for life in competition. Quantum of Indian blood alone should not determine management. Some full-bloods have better business sense than those of small degree of Indian blood. Character, education, business experience, environment, age, and all circumstances should be considered. Considerable number should have restrictions retained indefinitely. Estimates between 50 and 75 percent have made a success. Most failures come from 'easy money' attitude. Successes due to simple homely virtues.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Kiowa Indian Agency, Anadarko, Oklahoma
testimony.subject: Patents-in-fee at Kiowa Indian Agency
testimony.key_claims: Most important administrative function is deciding whether to recommend patent-in-fee. Granting control of estate prematurely subjects Indian to temptation and extravagant habits. Believes it is grossest mistake to issue patents based on blood status or educational qualifications alone. Has many full-blood Indians who cannot speak English whom he would rather trust with patent than educated young fellows. Of last sixty patents from Declaration of Policy, twenty were promptly mortgaged (only one released), sixteen sold outright, twenty-four clear but likely to be encumbered. In more than six years, can recall only one case of success. Recommends original allotment or at least 40 acres be inalienable during life of allottee with land taxable after trust period. Better to err by delaying patent than granting prematurely.

testimony.subject: Issuance of patents to Indians
testimony.key_claims: Convinced that reports of Indians selling lands and wasting proceeds are only too true, and probably only a portion of the full story. Going too fast in releasing Indians from government supervision and protection.

taxes.land_description: 40 acres reserved as homestead on original allotment
taxes.context: C. V. Stinchecum proposed that 40 acres be inalienable during allottee's lifetime but taxable at end of trust period; taxes could not be collected from that property but would be chargeable to other property the Indian might own
